content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Monday he is following through on his campaign promise of disbanding a group within the city’s police department that’s faced backlash over its aggressive tactics against protesters.

The Strategic Response Group “was tasked with both counterterrorism enforcement and protest response,” Mamdani said in a video. “Those are not the same, and they should be separated.”

In an effort to reshape the city’s approach to public safety, the mayor and New York City Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch said they will form new dialogue-focused units within the NYPD and the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety – including what Mamdani called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division.

“This will not be a uniformed police unit. It will be made up of civilians without weapons or arrest powers,” the mayor said of CDDD, which will take the lead in engaging with New Yorkers while the NYPD’s new First Amendment Support Team serves as a liaison unit for protest response. Trained officers can still be called upon to make arrests if needed, he added.

Mamdani also announced a ban on certain aggressive crowd control methods at protests, including the use of long guns, tear gas, pepper spray and kettling — a controversial tactic in which police surround protesters and physically confine them to a specific area.

Since its inception in 2015, the SRG has faced widespread backlash for using force and counterterrorism tactics against people exercising their right to protest. The unit, made up of hundreds of members, has been deployed in response to racial justice and pro-Palestinian protests.

“A unit trained in counterterrorism, the SRG readily suppressed dissent, escalated tensions and injured New Yorkers, costing the City millions for its abuses,” the NYCLU said in a statement. “The demise of the SRG is a victory for our First Amendment rights and the advocates who worked tirelessly for this day.”

However, the two groups also said the new police unit will require continued oversight and that they remain concerned about the restructuring.

Mamdani said his directive builds on New York City Councilmember Chi Ossé’s CURB Act. Ossé joined Mamdani in announcing the directive in Monday’s video.

“Government has a responsibility to both protect New Yorkers’ constitutional rights and keep our community safe,” Ossé said. “Those priorities are not in conflict; they are intertwined.”

The SRG’s counterterrorism functions, like the deployment of heavy weapons, will be folded into the NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau, according to Mamdani and Tisch. The commissioner said the new structure will preserve police’s ability to respond to serious threats while ensuring officers have more support during big events like protests.

“I believe strongly that the NYPD must always be willing to examine how we operate and make improvements,” Tisch said in a statement. “I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat. These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department.”
